title: tldr CLI is the only contract: parse only JSON output, never scrape text
description:
## Decision

All interaction with tldr-code happens via subprocess.run(["tldr", ...]).
We always pass '--json' (or equivalent structured-output flag) and parse
JSON. We never:
- Scrape human-readable text output
- Read tldr-code's internal databases (Salsa store, embedding cache)
- Link against tldr-code Rust crates
- Import tldr-code Python bindings (none exist today, but the rule
  pre-emptively forbids it)

## Rationale

JSON output is the only stable contract tldr-code publishes. Text output
is for humans and may change between minor versions without notice;
internal databases are implementation details. By restricting ourselves
to JSON CLI output, we get the strongest possible decoupling and the
clearest break signal if upstream ever removes a flag (we get an
unparseable response immediately, rather than silently misbehaving).

## Alternatives Considered

- **Scrape text output where JSON is not available**: Tolerated only as
  a last resort, and only with the tldr version pinned in service_state
  so we warn on mismatch. File an upstream issue requesting JSON for any
  command lacking it.
- **Read ~/.tldr/embeddings/cache.json directly**: Rejected. That file
  is tldr's internal cache format and not part of its public contract.
- **Use Rust FFI to call tldr-code functions**: Rejected. Couples us to
  internal Rust signatures and forces tldr-code recompilation on every
  upgrade.

## Affects

- service/tldr_cli.py is the only module that runs `tldr` subprocesses
- All callers use the typed wrappers in tldr_cli.py, never raw subprocess
- service_state.tldr_version_tested column tracks the pinned version

title: Vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry: emit standard OTLP, depend on no specific backend
description:
## Decision

tldr-management emits standard OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and logs via
OTLP (gRPC or HTTP). It never imports from, links to, or depends on any
specific observability backend (HyperDX, SigNoz, DataDog, Honeycomb,
Aspire, Jaeger, etc.). Backend selection is driven entirely by the
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT environment variable.

## Rationale

Vendor-lock-in is the largest hidden cost in observability. By committing
to pure OTel, we guarantee that any user can point the service at any
OTLP-compatible backend (open-source or SaaS) by changing one env var.
Migration between backends is a config change, not a code change. This
also keeps our dependency footprint clean — the optional OTel packages
total ~150KB and have no transitive vendor logos.

## Alternatives Considered

- **HyperDX-specific SDK (hyperdx pip package)**: Rejected. Even though
  HyperDX is the chosen personal visualization backend, embedding its SDK
  would couple our code to one vendor.
- **DataDog ddtrace, Honeycomb beeline, Sentry SDK**: Rejected for the
  same reason.
- **No telemetry at all**: Rejected. Forfeits observability of subprocess
  calls, embed durations, and watcher event rates.
- **Custom telemetry protocol**: Rejected. OTLP is the standard; rolling
  our own would require building exporters for every backend we want to
  support.

## Affects

- requirements: only opentelemetry-* packages, no vendor SDKs
- Code may use only `from opentelemetry import trace/metrics/logs`
- Reviewer rule: any PR adding a vendor-specific import is rejected
- README design principle #6 documents this rule

title: Event-driven re-indexing replaces 30-minute mtime polling
description:
## Decision

Re-embed changed files by reacting to file-watcher events (CHANGE/CREATE)
with a ~2-second debounce. Do NOT poll the filesystem on a timer.

## Rationale

The original DESIGN.md specified a 30-minute mtime + MD5 polling loop.
This means a file saved at minute 0 is not re-embedded until minute 30 in
the worst case. With fsnotifier giving us kernel-level events at <100ms
latency, we can re-embed within ~2 seconds of save (the debounce window
to coalesce editor atomic-save sequences and rapid sequential edits).
Zero CPU usage when idle vs scanning every 30 minutes.

## Alternatives Considered

- **30-minute mtime polling (original DESIGN.md)**: Rejected. Latency too
  high; constant CPU spikes every 30 min even when nothing changed.
- **git diff polling**: Rejected. Misses uncommitted edits and untracked
  files — exactly the files developers want re-indexed.
- **Inotify-only (Linux) with mtime polling on Mac/Win**: Rejected.
  fsnotifier handles all three platforms uniformly.
- **No debounce (re-embed on every event)**: Rejected. Editor
  atomic-saves emit CREATE+DELETE+CREATE in quick succession; embedding
  each would waste work.
- **5+ second debounce**: Considered. Settled on 2s as the user-perceived
  threshold — feels instant in practice.

## Affects

- service/scheduler.py debouncing logic
- DESIGN.md "Every 30 Minutes — Incremental Re-index" section must be
  rewritten
- Removes the periodic-scan code path entirely

title: JetBrains fsnotifier (vendored C source) as the file-watching backend
description:
## Decision

Use the JetBrains fsnotifier C source (Apache 2.0) as our file-watching
helper. Vendor the C source into vendor/watcher-src/ and compile it at
install time. The watcher is invoked as a subprocess by the Django service
and communicates via its line-based stdin/stdout protocol.

## Rationale

fsnotifier is the file-watching binary used by every JetBrains IDE
(IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, etc.) in production by millions of
developers. It wraps the OS-native event APIs (inotify on Linux, FSEvents
on macOS, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) with a tiny portable C layer
and a simple text protocol. It is event-driven (no polling), has handled
huge monorepos for over a decade, and is the smallest possible dependency
that gives us IDE-quality file watching.

## Alternatives Considered

- **chokidar (Node)**: Rejected. Wrong language; would require Node runtime.
- **@parcel/watcher (Node native addon)**: Rejected. Same Node runtime
  issue; the C++ core is good but the wrapper is Node-specific.
- **watchdog (Python)**: Rejected. Silently falls back to polling on
  unsupported filesystems (Docker bind mounts, NFS, SMB) — design rule
  forbids polling fallback.
- **watchfiles (Python, Rust-backed)**: Strong contender. Rejected because
  fsnotifier has a longer track record at IDE scale and is reusable from
  any language. Watchfiles remains a viable fallback if fsnotifier ever
  fails to build.
- **Raw inotify/FSEvents/ReadDirectoryChangesW**: Rejected. Three
  per-platform implementations to maintain; fsnotifier already does this.
- **Watchman (Meta's daemon)**: Rejected. Overkill for single-user; runs
  as a separate daemon and adds operational complexity.
- **efsw / wtr/watcher / libuv (C++ libraries)**: Rejected. None has the
  battle-testing of fsnotifier; building our own wrapper adds maintenance.

## Affects

- vendor/watcher-src/ contains JetBrains fsnotifier source (Apache 2.0)
- service/watcher.py implements the Python-side protocol parser
- Build requires clang (see related decision)
- Event types CHANGE/CREATE/DELETE/DIRTY/RECDIRTY/RESET flow into our
  scheduler

title: SQLite is the only supported database; no PostgreSQL hard dependency
description:
## Decision

Use SQLite (via Django's default backend) as the sole supported database.
Explicitly do NOT support PostgreSQL, MySQL, or any other database. No
external database server, ever.

## Rationale

tldr-management runs as a single-user local service. Everything lives in a
single state.db file under .tldr-svc/. This keeps the runtime footprint to
Python + one SQLite file + one C binary. No server processes to install,
configure, run, or back up. The entire installation can be removed with
'rm -rf .tldr-svc/'.

## Alternatives Considered

- **PostgreSQL (matches Stock-Monitor-Django stack)**: Rejected. Adds a
  server process, psycopg binary, connection pool, and external lifecycle.
  Overkill for single-user local state.
- **DuckDB**: Rejected. Excellent for analytics but adds a non-trivial
  dependency for no benefit — our writes are tiny key-value + log appends.
- **JSON files on disk**: Rejected. No ORM, no migrations, no admin, no
  transactional safety.
- **Make the database swappable via settings**: Rejected. Premature
  flexibility; would require maintaining tests against multiple backends.

## Affects

- settings.py DATABASES configuration
- All ORM models (must stay SQLite-compatible)
- Excluded deps: psycopg, psycopg-pool, psycopg-binary

title: Python + Django as the management layer language and framework
description:
## Decision

Implement tldr-management in Python using the Django web framework.

## Rationale

The performance-critical path (file watching) is delegated to a C binary that
runs at kernel speed. Everything else — subprocess management, SQLite writes,
dashboard rendering — operates at sub-second resolution where Python's
per-call overhead is irrelevant. Django gives us ORM + migrations + admin +
management commands + DRF + HTMX templates for free, all running over the
same stdlib logging and signal handling we already use.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Pure stdlib Python (no framework)**: Rejected. We would re-implement
  migrations, admin UI, request routing, and dashboard rendering by hand.
- **Node.js**: Rejected. Adds a separate runtime and dependency tree the
  user's ecosystem does not standardize on.
- **Rust**: Rejected. Overkill for orchestration; the hot path is already in
  C/Rust elsewhere.
- **Go**: Rejected. Not in the user's existing stack; lacks Django's batteries.
- **Flask / FastAPI**: Rejected. Lighter, but we lose ORM, admin, migrations,
  and management commands — all of which we want.

## Affects

- Entire codebase language choice
- Dependency footprint
- Developer onboarding (Django familiarity is widely available)

title: Sidecar/wrapper architecture: tldr-management never modifies tldr-code Rust source
description:
## Decision

tldr-management is implemented as a sidecar/wrapper that drives the upstream
tldr-code Rust CLI exclusively through its public CLI (subprocess + --json
output). The fork of tldr-code stays as close to upstream as humanly possible
(ideally zero source-code changes) so 'git pull upstream main' is always a
fast-forward.

## Rationale

The upstream tldr-code author is not accepting external contributions. To
benefit from ongoing upstream improvements while still shipping our own ideas,
we need an integration boundary that does not couple to internal Rust crates
or file layouts. The CLI is the only stable, public contract; treating it as
our integration surface guarantees that internal refactors upstream never
break our layer.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Hard fork with substantial in-tree modifications**: Rejected. Every
  upstream pull becomes a multi-hour merge-conflict session. Long-term
  untenable.
- **Contribute features upstream**: Rejected. Upstream is closed to external
  contributions.
- **Runtime overlay / monkey-patching of tldr-code internals**: Rejected.
  Internal APIs are not stable and not part of the published contract; would
  break silently on upstream refactors.
- **Link against tldr-code Rust crates via Cargo**: Rejected. Couples us to
  internal types; cargo workspace changes upstream would force rebuilds and
  type-signature updates.

## Affects

- Every component of tldr-management
- All future feature work must be implemented in our layer, never in the fork
- Implies: no import of tldr-code modules, no parsing of internal files, no
  scraping of human-readable output

title: Scaffold test suite folder structure
description: Initialize tests/ with conftest.py, unit/integration/e2e subdirectories, skip decorators, and pytest marks. No application code yet — stubs only, ready to fill in as service/ modules are built.
close_reason: Folder structure created: unit/, integration/, e2e/ with __init__.py, conftest.py with skip conditions, pytest.ini with marks. No stub files.

title: Test fixture: sparse-clone JetBrains fsnotifier via bash script; no git submodules
description:
## Decision

Test fixtures are prepared via a single bash script (scripts/prepare-test-case.sh) that performs a **sparse git clone** of JetBrains/intellij-community, materializing only the native/fsNotifier/ subdirectory into tests/fixtures/fsnotifier/. The fixture directory is gitignored (with a loud "NEVER ADD" comment) except for a tracked README.md that documents the rule.

Do NOT use git submodules. Do NOT commit fixture contents to the repo.

## Rationale

Three constraints drove the choice:

1. **Tests need a real, sizeable codebase** to exercise tldr warm / embed / semantic against — synthetic fixtures hide real-world bugs.
2. **Semantic indexing must finish fast** during the test run (the user tried udhaya10/tldr-code as a fixture earlier and rejected it for being too slow to index).
3. **New contributors must not learn submodule mechanics** or face "why is this empty?" issues from forgetting --recurse-submodules.

A sparse clone of native/fsNotifier/ gives us:
- ~14 files, ~76 KB — semantic indexing finishes in seconds
- Real production-grade C source used by every JetBrains IDE (millions of devs)
- Dogfooding: it is literally the same source we vendor as our runtime file-watcher helper
- C-language coverage in the embedder (beyond Python/TS)
- Apache 2.0 license — freely redistributable

The script (prepare-test-case.sh) is idempotent and supports --update, --clean, --sha <commit>, --help. Pinning a SHA via TLDR_TEST_SHA gives us reproducibility equivalent to a submodule lockfile, without the submodule footguns.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Git submodule of JetBrains/intellij-community**: Rejected. Submodules are a recurring source of "I forgot --recurse-submodules" bugs. Adds clone time and friction for contributors who never run tests. SHA pinning is replicable in 20 lines of bash.
- **Git submodule of just native/fsNotifier/ (partial clone via submodule)**: Rejected. Submodules don't support sparse checkout cleanly; same friction without the simplicity benefit.
- **Git subtree**: Rejected. Merges upstream history into our repo — bloats clone size permanently.
- **Vendoring (copy fsnotifier source into our repo)**: Rejected. Snapshots go stale; we already vendor the runtime helper version, and mixing test/runtime concerns is messy.
- **Use udhaya10/tldr-code as the fixture**: Rejected. Initially considered (it is the upstream we wrap), but semantic indexing of its full Rust corpus is too slow for fast test loops. Also philosophically circular: testing tldr-code with tldr-code can hide bugs that are invisible to itself.
- **Use a synthetic, hand-crafted small fixture committed to the repo**: Rejected. Synthetic fixtures do not exercise real-world patterns (long files, mixed languages, deep directories). Misses bugs.
- **Use a hybrid (committed small + fetched large fixtures)**: Considered. Rejected for now to keep the surface minimal — one script, one fixture path. Can be added later if a second corpus proves necessary.
- **Use a larger JetBrains repo (intellij-community in full, kotlin, ideavim)**: Rejected. All are too large for fast semantic indexing — they would have the same slowness problem we rejected udhaya10/tldr-code for.
- **CI clones fixture inline (no script)**: Rejected. Local dev would diverge from CI; the script unifies both paths.

## Affects

- scripts/prepare-test-case.sh (the fetcher)
- tests/fixtures/ (the fixture directory)
- tests/fixtures/README.md (the only tracked file inside; explains the NEVER-ADD rule)
- .gitignore (blocks tests/fixtures/* with comment, except README.md)
- All future tests that need a real-world corpus must use tests/fixtures/fsnotifier/native/fsNotifier/ via the shared pytest fixture
- CI workflow must run prepare-test-case.sh before the test job and cache tests/fixtures/ between runs
- Replaces (would have been) Phase 0 of the testing roadmap — fixture system is done before any test is written

title: Service state lives in project-local .tldr-svc/; never write inside ~/.tldr/
description:
## Decision

All tldr-management runtime state (SQLite DB, PID lock, log file,
compiled watcher binary, vendored C source if extracted) lives under a
project-local .tldr-svc/ directory. We never write to ~/.tldr/ or any
other directory owned by tldr-code. Read-only reads of tldr-owned paths
(e.g., 'ls ~/.tldr/embeddings/' to detect cold cache) are permitted.

## Rationale

Owning a separate directory means our state is per-project, easy to wipe
('rm -rf .tldr-svc/'), and never collides with tldr-code's own
on-disk layout. If tldr-code reorganizes its own state directory in a
future release, our service is unaffected. This is a direct consequence
of the sidecar architecture decision.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Write inside ~/.tldr/**: Rejected. Couples us to tldr's directory
  layout; tldr might wipe its own directory on version upgrades.
- **Use OS-standard XDG paths (~/.local/share/tldr-management/)**:
  Rejected for the first phase — being project-local is more useful for
  developers who want per-repo state. Can revisit if multi-project
  support is added.
- **Use a system-wide /var/lib path**: Rejected. Requires root or
  systemd integration; we are a userspace tool.

## Affects

- All file paths in service code use .tldr-svc/ prefix
- .gitignore must include .tldr-svc/
- README documents the cleanup command 'rm -rf .tldr-svc/'

title: Minimal required dependency stack: 6 packages plus optional observability
description:
## Decision

Required runtime dependencies (pinned):
- django==6.0.5
- djangorestframework==3.17.1
- cashews==7.5.0
- filelock==3.29.0
- tenacity==9.1.4
- python-dotenv==1.2.2

Optional observability dependencies (install only if telemetry is wanted):
- opentelemetry-distro
- opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
- opentelemetry-instrumentation-django
- opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging
- python-json-logger

Total required: 6 packages. Anything else must be justified case-by-case.

## Rationale

A small dependency surface means fewer security updates, faster pip
installs, smaller wheel cache, and less behavior surprise from transitive
dep upgrades. Every package on the list earns its slot:
- django, drf: web layer + JSON API
- cashews: async cache wrapper for daemon-status calls
- filelock: cross-process PID lock (replaces hand-rolled approach)
- tenacity: retry decorator for flaky subprocess calls
- python-dotenv: .env loading (matches existing ecosystem convention)

## Alternatives Considered

- **Add Procrastinate / Celery / etc.**: Rejected — see scheduling
  decision.
- **Add psycopg / PostgreSQL stack**: Rejected — see SQLite decision.
- **Add Channels / Daphne / Uvicorn for WebSocket dashboard**: Rejected.
  WSGI works fine for status polling; WebSocket can be added later if a
  live dashboard ever proves necessary.
- **Add httpx for outbound HTTP**: Deferred. We have no outbound HTTP
  calls today; stdlib urllib suffices if any are added.
- **Add requests**: Same as httpx.
- **Add pydantic for schema validation**: Deferred. Django models +
  serializers cover validation today; pydantic only enters if we add a
  non-Django API surface.

## Affects

- pyproject.toml / requirements.txt
- README dependency table
- Any PR adding a new top-level dependency requires a decision update

title: Logging stack: stdlib logging + python-json-logger + opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging
description:
## Decision

Use Python stdlib logging as the API. Optionally enhance with
python-json-logger (JSON formatter, ~30KB) and
opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging (injects trace_id/span_id into
LogRecord attributes). No loguru, no structlog, no parallel logging
system.

## Rationale

Django, DRF, and OpenTelemetry all hook into stdlib logging natively.
Choosing anything else creates an impedance mismatch where some logs flow
through stdlib and others through the alternative library. The three-
layer composition (stdlib + OTel handler + JSON formatter) is clean: each
layer has exactly one job, and disabling any layer leaves the rest
functional.

## Alternatives Considered

- **loguru**: Rejected. Pretty syntax, but creates a parallel logging
  system. Bridging back to stdlib (which Django and OTel require) is
  fragile.
- **structlog**: Rejected. Excellent key-value pipeline, but OTel span
  attributes already cover structured context for traced operations. The
  extra layer earns nothing.
- **picologging (Microsoft)**: Rejected. ~5% faster but a C extension
  with no benefit at our log volume.
- **Plain stdlib without JSON or OTel**: Acceptable fallback. JSON and
  OTel are optional features in our config.

## Affects

- tldr_management/settings.py LOGGING dict (~30 lines)
- All code uses `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` directly
- Optional deps: python-json-logger, opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging

title: stdlib threading.Timer for scheduling; no Celery, Procrastinate, or task queue
description:
## Decision

Implement the two scheduled jobs (10-minute daemon health check, debounced
embed batch processor) using Python stdlib threading.Timer inside the
long-running service process. Do NOT introduce a task queue or background
job framework.

## Rationale

The service is a single long-running process with exactly two periodic
concerns:
1. Heartbeat every 10 minutes against the tldr daemon
2. Drain the debounced embed queue every ~2 seconds

Both can be expressed in ~30 lines of stdlib code. A task queue would add
a broker, a worker process, serialization overhead, and an entire mental
model for no benefit.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Celery + Redis/RabbitMQ**: Rejected. Adds a broker process we do not
  need; massive operational complexity for two timers.
- **Procrastinate (PostgreSQL-backed, used in Stock-Monitor-Django)**:
  Rejected. Requires PostgreSQL (excluded by another decision) and is
  designed for distributed worker pools, not single-process schedulers.
- **Django-Q / Huey**: Rejected. Lighter than Celery but still a job
  framework with worker pools and a database queue we do not need.
- **APScheduler**: Rejected. Closest fit, but still an external dep that
  adds nothing over threading.Timer for our use case.

## Affects

- service/scheduler.py uses threading.Timer
- No worker process to spawn or manage
- service.py runs as a single foreground process under systemd / launchd

title: clang is the only required C compiler across Linux, macOS, and Windows
description:
## Decision

Standardize on clang as the single required C compiler for building the
vendored file-watcher binary. Do NOT auto-detect or support gcc, MSVC,
or other compilers.

## Rationale

clang is the only C compiler available via a single official install step
on all three platforms: macOS (Xcode CLT), Linux (apt/dnf/pacman), Windows
(MSYS2 or LLVM installer). Standardizing on one compiler means identical
flags, identical error messages, identical build script across all
platforms — no per-OS branches, no makefile variants, no MSBuild config.

## Alternatives Considered

- **gcc**: Rejected. Not a single-step install on Windows; MinGW or MSYS2
  required, which is what we already require for clang.
- **MSVC (cl.exe)**: Rejected. Windows-only; would need a separate
  Linux/Mac toolchain anyway.
- **Auto-detect any C99 compiler (clang/gcc/cl.exe)**: Rejected. Adds
  detection branches in the build script, more failure modes, harder to
  reproduce bugs. We trade flexibility for simplicity.
- **Zig cc**: Considered. Single binary, cross-platform, but adds a
  non-mainstream dependency for marginal gain.

## Affects

- scripts/build-watcher.sh
- README requirements section
- Vendored C source must be clang-compatible (which it is — JetBrains
  fsnotifier compiles cleanly with clang)

title: Use latest stable Python (3.14) and Django (6.0), not LTS
description:
## Decision

Pin minimum versions to Python 3.14+ and Django 6.0+ (latest stable as of
project inception in 2026). Explicitly do NOT target Django 5.2 LTS or
Python 3.13 or earlier.

## Rationale

We are a greenfield, single-user developer tool. There is no production fleet
to support, no compliance window, no legacy users. Tracking latest stable
gives us access to performance improvements (Python 3.14 JIT, free-threaded
mode), new typing features, and the longest forward runway before the next
forced upgrade.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Django 5.2 LTS + Python 3.13**: Rejected. LTS pinning trades performance
  and features for stability we do not need. We will simply track latest
  stable as new versions ship.
- **Django 4.2 LTS (older LTS)**: Rejected. Reaching EOL April 2026.
- **Allow Python 3.11+ broadly**: Rejected. Forces us to support older
  syntax and miss type-hint improvements; no real benefit.

## Affects

- requirements.txt minimum pins
- README requirements section
- CI matrix

title: REJECTED: polling-based file watching (anti-pattern to remember)
description:
## Decision (REJECTED)

This is a record of an explicitly REJECTED approach so future contributors
do not re-propose it.

REJECTED: any form of polling-based file change detection — including
mtime polling, content-hash polling, fs.watchFile, Django's StatReloader,
watchdog's PollingObserver, or any "fallback to polling" path.

## Rationale for Rejection

- High latency: typical polling intervals (1s minimum, 30s common) miss
  the "feels instant" UX threshold.
- Constant CPU drain even when nothing changes (the OS does not get to
  sleep the process).
- Scans scale linearly with file count; large monorepos become
  prohibitively expensive.
- Silent fallback (watchdog's PollingObserver auto-engages on unsupported
  filesystems) creates "works on my machine" bugs.

## Alternatives (what we DO instead)

- fsnotifier (event-driven via inotify/FSEvents/RDCW)
- See "JetBrains fsnotifier" decision

## Affects

- service/watcher.py must never instantiate a polling watcher
- If fsnotifier fails to build, the service must error loudly rather
  than silently degrading
- README explicitly forbids polling fallback

title: REJECTED: vendor-specific telemetry SDKs (anti-pattern to remember)
description:
## Decision (REJECTED)

This is a record of an explicitly REJECTED approach so future contributors
do not re-propose it.

REJECTED: importing vendor-specific Python SDKs for observability backends
(hyperdx, ddtrace, honeycomb-beeline, sentry-sdk, etc.) instead of using
standard OpenTelemetry over OTLP.

## Rationale for Rejection

Vendor SDKs couple our code to a single backend. They typically:
- Pull in non-OTel transitive dependencies
- Add vendor-specific configuration alongside OTel env vars
- Make migration to another backend a code change rather than a config
  change
- Sometimes monkey-patch stdlib or third-party libraries in ways that
  conflict with OTel auto-instrumentation

Even when the chosen backend (HyperDX in our case) ships an SDK that is
"easier" or has "better defaults", we forgo it to preserve neutrality.

## Alternatives Considered (i.e., what we DO instead)

- Pure opentelemetry-* packages
- OTLP exporter
- Env-var-driven endpoint selection

## Affects

- README Observability section's "design rule for contributors" code
  example
- Code review checklist: reject any PR adding `import hyperdx`, `import
  ddtrace`, `import sentry_sdk`, etc.

title: Plain WSGI + HTMX templates for the dashboard; no Django Channels or SPA
description:
## Decision

The status dashboard is served over plain Django WSGI using server-
rendered templates with HTMX for incremental updates. Do NOT use Django
Channels, WebSockets, ASGI, Daphne/Uvicorn, or a JavaScript SPA in the
first phase.

## Rationale

The dashboard refreshes every few seconds with a handful of status fields
and a recent-events list. HTMX with polling (hx-trigger="every 2s") is
sufficient and adds zero JS frameworks, zero ASGI server, zero WebSocket
protocol management. Less code, less to break, faster to ship.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Django Channels + WebSocket live updates**: Rejected for phase 1.
  Adds Daphne/Uvicorn, channel layers, and an async runtime. Can be
  added later if 2-second polling proves visibly stale (unlikely).
- **React/Vue/Svelte SPA**: Rejected. Build pipeline, bundler, JS
  toolchain — all for a single status page. HTMX gives us 80% of the
  interactive feel for 1% of the complexity.
- **CLI-only status (no web UI)**: Rejected. We want a glanceable
  always-on dashboard, not just a one-shot command.

## Affects

- service/views.py uses Django template responses
- requirements does NOT include channels, daphne, uvicorn
- Single htmx.min.js shipped as a static asset

title: HyperDX as the recommended local visualization backend (personal choice, not product dependency)
description:
## Decision

For local development, HyperDX is the recommended observability backend
for visualizing tldr-management traces, metrics, and logs. This is a
personal/tooling recommendation only — the product itself is
backend-agnostic (see vendor-neutral OTel decision).

## Rationale

HyperDX provides the richest UI among the open-source OTLP-receiving
options: unified search bar across traces/logs/metrics, session-replay-
style trace timelines, Lucene-style query syntax, saved dashboards.
For investigating "why was this embed slow" questions, it is materially
better than Aspire Dashboard or Jaeger. It is open source, self-hostable
via Docker Compose, and speaks pure OTLP.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Aspire Dashboard (Microsoft)**: Strong alternative for ephemeral dev
  setups (single Docker command, no persistence). Considered but lacks
  exploration features and persistence. Listed as fully-supported in
  README.
- **SigNoz**: Comparable feature set, slightly less polished UI. Heavier
  ClickHouse footprint.
- **Uptrace, OpenObserve**: Lighter but smaller feature sets.
- **Jaeger**: Traces only, no metrics — incomplete for our needs.
- **DataDog, Honeycomb, New Relic, Grafana Cloud**: SaaS, overkill for
  single-user dev tool.

## Affects

- README documentation only — code remains backend-neutral
- Setup-guide section in README may include HyperDX-specific docker run
  instructions
- If HyperDX requirements ever leak into the product code, this decision
  is invalid and must be reversed
